WMI.about.description: used to manage both local and remote computers.
WMI.about.who: WMI is the Microsoft (WBEM) WebBased Enterprise Management.

WMI.cmdlets.description: these cmdlets manage local and remote computers.
WMI.cmdlets.Get-WmiObject: Gets instances of WMI classes or information about the available classes.
WMI.cmdlets.Set-WmiInstance: Creates or modifies instances of WMI classes.

WMI.samples.description2: displays information about the WinRM service for three remote computers

WMI.remoting.feature1: WMI management of local systems is useful.
WMI.remoting.feature2: WMI remoting capabilities is a powerful administrative tool.
WMI.remoting.DCOM connections: (DCOM) Distributed Component Object Model is used to connect to and manage systems
WMI.remoting.weakness: WMI can be blocked by firewalls and locked-down DCOM permissions

WMI.type_accelerators.description: shortcuts which allow more direct access to WMI objects

[wmisearcher].application: creates a searcher you can do a Get() on.

WMI.troubleshooting.situation: common problems trying to connect remotely

Problem 1.statement: WMI cannot connect to offline remote computers
Problem 1.error_message: Remote server machine does not exist or is unavailable
Problem 1.solution: Try to ping the remote computer

Problem 2.statement: local admin rights are required on remote computers.
Problem 2.error: If you do not, access to that computer will be denied.

solution.step2: Computer Management -> Services and Applications -> WMI Control -> Properties.
solution.step3: WMI Control Properties dialog box, click the Security tab

Problem 3.statement: A firewall is blocking access to the remote computer
Problem 3.description: By default windows firewalls rejects incoming WMI requests blocking all unsolicited network traffic including DCOM, WMI and RPC traffic.
Problem 3.error_message: Remote server machine does not exist or is unavailable

about_WQL.WQL.benefits: WQL is faster than Get-WmiObject commands

Get-CimInstance.description3: The CIM cmdlets perform the same tasks as the WMI cmdlets.
Get-CimInstance.description4: CIM enables cmdlets to use the same techniques to manage Windows computers and other operating systems.

[wmisearcher].description: This lets you query WMI and to configure the way the query is conducted.
[wmisearcher].description1: [wmisearcher] gives easy access to the ManagementObjectSearcher .NET class.
[wmisearcher].description2: [wmisearcher] creates a ManagementObjectSearcher object from a WQL statement string.
[wmisearcher].description3: The ManagementObjectSearcher object has many properties and methods
[wmisearcher].description4: The Get method invokes WMI queries and returning objects.

use1.1: Cast the WQL string into a ManagementObjectSearcher object
use1.2: Call the Get method of the ManagementObjectSearcher object

[wmisearcher].use2: [wmisearcher] can be used to cast queries and variables.
[wmisearcher].use3: gets Name property of the Win32_BIOS WMI class

WHERE.use: property name and value must be accurate (notepad not notepad.exe)

Operators.comparison.ISA: Evaluates a member of a WMI class
Operators.comparison.fact: WQL operators can be used in the -Filter parameter
Operators.comparison.exampleOne: $getWmiObjectSplat = @{ Class = 'Win32_Process'; Property = 'Name', 'ProcessId'; Filter = 'ProcessId >= 1004'}; Get-WmiObject @getWmiObjectSplat | Sort-Object ProcessId | Select-Object Name, ProcessId -Last 5

usage.1: get the last five processes with ProcessId -gt than 1004.
usage.2: The Filter parameter is used to specify the condition.

LIKE.description: LIKE allows filtering with wildcard patterns

fact.a: LIKE behaves like equals (=) when used without range or wildcards,
fact.b: returning objects only when they're an exact pattern matches.

[].usage: search for anof the Win32_Process class instances with names [H-N]
[].exampleOne: Notepad; $query = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE Name LIKE '[H-N]otepad.exe'"; Get-WmiObject -Query $query | select Name, ProcessId;

[]%.fact: range can be combined with percent (%) for simple/powerful filters.
[]%.example2: Get-WmiObject -Query $query | Select-Object -Property Name, ProcessId | Sort-Object -Property Name

usage.Pipeline1: select process names begining between [A-P] followed by zero or more letters.

[]%.exampleOne: $query = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE name LIKE '[A-P]%'"; Get-WmiObject -Query $query | Select-Object -Property Name, ProcessId | Sort-Object -Property Name

^.example2: Get-WmiObject -Query $query | Select-Object -Property Name, ProcessId | Sort-Object -Property Name
^.usage: search for an  of the Win32_Process class instances with names [H-N]
^.exampleOne: $query = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE name LIKE '[^ASWPRCUN]%'"; Get-WmiObject -Query $query | Select-Object -Property Name, ProcessId | Sort-Object -Property Name;

%.fact: In WQL (%) is identical to (*) in PowerShell.
%.usage: get process names that begin with calc.
%.exampleOne: $query = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE Name LIKE 'calc%'"; Get-WmiObject -Query $query | Select-Object -Property Name, ProcessId

_.usage: get process names with the pattern c_lc.exe
_.exampleOne: $query = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE Name LIKE 'c_lc.exe'"; Get-WmiObject -Query $query | Select-Object -Property Name, ProcessId

Exact match.fact: Matches without wildcards require exact matches
Exact match.exampleOne: $query = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE name LIKE 'WLIDSVC.exe'"; Get-WmiObject -Query $query | Select-Object -Property Name, ProcessId

OR.fact1: The OR keyword appears in the WHERE clause.
OR.fact4: The OR statement can be used with more than two conditions.
OR.returns: returns items using an inclusive OR operation of 2+ conditions
OR.example1b: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE Name='winword.exe' OR Name='excel.exe'
OR.usage: returns winword.exe OR excel.exe out of all Win32_Process instances.
OR.example2b: ([wmisearcher]"select * from win32_process where name='winword.exe' OR name='excel.exel'").Get()
OR.example1One: start-process winword.exe, excel.exe; $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE Name='winword.exe' OR Name='excel.exe'; Get-WmiObject -Query $q
OR.example2One: start-process winword.exe, excel.exe, powershell.exe; ([wmisearcher]"select * from win32_process where name='winword.exe' OR name='excel.exel'").Get()

AND.fact1: AND specifies multiple related conditions in he WHERE clause.
AND.fact2: All operators are valid with OR & AND operators

combination clauses.description: OR & AND operators may be combined in queries with
combination clauses.requirements: parentheses indicating which clauses to process first

AND.example1a: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE Name = 'winword.exe' AND ProcessId =6512"
AND.usage: get processes named Winword.exe with an ID of 6512.
AND.exampleOne: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE Name = 'winword.exe' AND ProcessId =6512"; Get-CimInstance -Query $q

Searching for null values.fact1: Some WMI class properties are initialized and others aren't
Searching for null values.fact2: a search for null might not work for all properties.
Searching for null values.fact3: gets processes with a null value for the IntallDate property.
Searching for null values.example1: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_Process WHERE InstallDate IS null"; Get-WmiObject -Query $q
Searching for null values.example2: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_UserAccount WHERE Description IS null"; Get-WmiObject -Query $q

usage2.1: get user accounts with a null value for the Description property.
usage2.2: This command doesn't return any user accounts
usage2.3: most user accounts don't have a Description property

usage3.1: gets user accounts without a Description property value
usage3.2: an equality operator with single quotes returns no value, not NULL.

Using true or false.usage1: return local user accounts from a domain joined computer.
Using true or false.example1One: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_UserAccount WHERE LocalAccount = True"; Get-CimInstance -Query $q
Using true or false.example2One: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_UserAccount WHERE LocalAccount = False"; Get-CimInstance -Query $q

Using the escape character.fact1: WQL uses backslashes (\) as Escape characters.
Using the escape character.fact2: PowerShell uses backticks (`) as Escape characters.
Using the escape character.fact3: Quotation marks need to be escaped in strings.
Using the escape character.fact4: backslashes need to be escaped in strings.

usage1.1: To finds a username including a single quote
usage1.2: a backslash escapes a single quote

Using the escape character.usage2: a backslash is escaped preventing an error.
Using the escape character.example1One: $q = "SELECT * FROM Win32_UserAccount WHERE Name = 'Tim O\'Brian'"; Get-CimInstance -Query $q
